title: NATO plan for drone-infested battlefield: AI flies, humans strike
excerpt: NATO is incorporating drones and artificial intelligence into a new defensive initiative aimed at fortifying its eastern flank.
content_html:
NATO plans to fortify its eastern edge using drones, sensors, and artificial intelligence in a massive network designed to spot and help repel a potential Russian attack.

As part of that plan, some systems may increasingly operate autonomously; however, humans will still decide what targets they engage.

Western officials say that the NATO alliance is exploring AI-assisted drone operations as part of the broad effort to bolster its defenses. The aim, however, isn't full autonomy; instead, machines could help pilot the drones, while human operators ultimately make the call on what they strike.

The approach echoes Ukraine's pursuits. The embattled country is increasingly incorporating AI into its drone operations, but both soldiers and defense tech firms have emphasized that humans must remain at the center of the fight, even as the war becomes more robotic.

For NATO, AI-assisted drones would be part of the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative, a digital battlespace network that the alliance is building to track threats along its borders with Russia and Belarus, which stretch from northern Finland down to the Black Sea.

The new concept will include thousands of drones, sensors, satellites, and artificial intelligence designed to detect potential breaches of allied territory and repel attacks as the first line of defense. Conventional military forces, such as tanks, fighter jets, and artillery, will remain the backbone.

US Army Maj. Ben Schiff, a software operations officer, told BILD — which, like Business Insider, is part of Axel Springer's Global Reporters Network — that both Ukraine and Russia still rely on humans to control drones. While some systems have artificial intelligence or machine-learning capabilities that allow brief moments of autonomy in flight, piloting is primarily performed by operators on the ground.

"What we're trying to do is kind of reverse the concept," Schiff said at the US Army Europe and Africa headquarters in Wiesbaden, Germany.

Schiff, a product manager for the EFDI Data Backbone, is the primary architect for the digital 'nervous system' that federates national systems across the alliance.

He said that "the most boring parts of flying"— drones loitering above the battlefield looking for targets — should be automated. When it comes to deciding what the drone should strike, though, that's where a human comes into play.

"So the humans are deciding what the drone does, but they don't necessarily need to take the action of flying it because we don't have a million pilots," he said. "We can't fly a million drones at the same time,"

Instead, AI-assisted flight can free up operators to focus solely on making targeting and engagement decisions.

EFDI is intended to help move NATO beyond a linear "kill chain" to a decentralized "kill web," where data from sensors can be rapidly passed to weapons systems and operators.

Often described as a "data highway," the system allows nations to "plug and play" their existing systems into a shared environment without custom integrations. The concept has already been validated in combat; US forces in the Middle East recently used the same type of data-sharing architecture to coordinate the first American combat kill of an Iranian Shahed drone in Kuwait with the Merops interceptor system.

"The value of a drone, sensor, or other capability is not determined solely by its individual performance," said Maj. Matt Blubaugh, a spokesperson for US Army Europe and Africa. "Its effectiveness depends on how well it integrates into the broader operational ecosystem."

Ukraine is playing a significant role in pioneering the integration of AI into military operations. In March, for instance, the country's defense ministry launched a first-of-its-kind program to incorporate AI into defense processes.

On the battlefield, Ukraine has made substantial progress in using AI to support functions such as decision-making, drone navigation, terminal guidance, and precision, said Andrii Hrytseniuk, the CEO of the Ukrainian state-backed innovation platform Brave1.

Hrytseniuk told Business Insider in Kyiv this spring that more than 200 local companies at the time were developing AI-based components for drones, missiles, radars, and other systems.

Ukrainian defense companies are integrating AI into their products to varying degrees. Many insist that machines won't control drones from start to finish.

Wild Hornets, manufacturer of the popular Sting interceptor drones, told Business Insider in May that AI will be gradually integrated at almost every stage of flight operations: target detection, identification, and, later, terminal guidance.

A spokesperson for the company said humans will still make the decision on what they strike. Since Russia is constantly changing its tactics, interceptor operators must keep tabs on these changes and make necessary adjustments, they said.

As autonomous systems become more common on the battlefield in Ukraine, commanders similarly told Business Insider that humans need to remain in the loop.

Ground robots, for instance, are increasingly replacing soldiers and taking on front-line logistics roles that have become extremely deadly. The push toward machines is intended to save lives, but not remove humans entirely from the battlefield, the Ukrainian commanders said.

Grek, a robot company commander with the 21st Unmanned Systems "Kraken" Regiment, who requested to be identified only by his call sign, said the goal is to "allow people to focus on the tasks where human judgment has the greatest value."

US Army officers stressed that NATO is using the operational environment in Ukraine to inform military planning for a potential future confrontation.

"We're not copying Ukraine," said Capt. Ronan Sefton. "We're learning from Ukraine."

sentences.en: Ukraine
sentences.zh: 乌克兰

content_html_zh:
北约计划在一个庞大的网络中使用无人机、传感器和人工智能来强化其东部边缘，该网络旨在发现并帮助击退俄罗斯的潜在攻击。

作为该计划的一部分，一些系统可能会越来越多地自主运行；然而，人类仍然会决定他们攻击的目标。

西方官员表示，北约联盟正在探索人工智能辅助的无人机行动，作为加强其防御的广泛努力的一部分。 然而，目标并不是完全自治；而是完全自治。相反，机器可以帮助驾驶无人机，而人类操作员最终可以根据无人机的攻击目标做出决定。

这一做法呼应了乌克兰的追求。 这个陷入困境的国家越来越多地将人工智能纳入其无人机操作中，但士兵和国防技术公司都强调，即使战争变得更加机器人化，人类也必须保持在战斗的中心。

对于北约来说，人工智能辅助无人机将成为“东侧威慑计划”的一部分，该计划是北约正在建立的数字战场网络，旨在跟踪其与俄罗斯和白俄罗斯边境沿线的威胁，这些边境从芬兰北部一直延伸到黑海。

新概念将包括数千架无人机、传感器、卫星和人工智能，旨在检测盟军领土的潜在突破并作为第一道防线击退攻击。 坦克、战斗机、火炮等常规军事力量仍将是骨干力量。

美国陆军少校 软件运营官本·希夫 (Ben Schiff) 告诉《图片报》——该报和《商业内幕》一样，都是阿克塞尔·施普林格全球记者网络的一部分——乌克兰和俄罗斯仍然依靠人类来控制无人机。 虽然一些系统具有人工智能或机器学习功能，允许在飞行中短暂自主，但驾驶主要由地面操作员执行。

希夫在德国威斯巴登的美国陆军欧洲和非洲总部表示：“我们正在尝试做的是扭转这一概念。”

Schiff 是 EFDI Data Backbone 的产品经理，也是联合整个联盟的国家系统的数字“神经系统”的主要架构师。

他说，“飞行中最无聊的部分”——无人机在战场上空徘徊寻找目标——应该实现自动化。 然而，当谈到决定无人机应该攻击什么时，这就是人类发挥作用的地方。

“因此，人类正在决定无人机的用途，但他们不一定需要采取驾驶无人机的行动，因为我们没有一百万飞行员，”他说。 “我们无法同时驾驶一百万架无人机，”

相反，人工智能辅助飞行可以让操作员专注于制定目标和交战决策。

EFDI 旨在帮助北约超越线性“杀伤链”，转向分散的“杀伤网络”，来自传感器的数据可以快速传递到武器系统和操作员。

该系统通常被描述为“数据高速公路”，允许各国将其现有系统“即插即用”到共享环境中，而无需定制集成。 这个概念已经在战斗中得到了验证；驻中东的美军最近使用相同类型的数据共享架构，利用 Merops 拦截系统协调美国在科威特首次对一架伊朗 Shahed 无人机进行战斗击落。

“无人机、传感器或其他功能的价值不仅仅取决于其单独的性能，”少校说。 马特·布鲁博（Matt Blubaugh），美国陆军欧洲和非洲发言人。 “它的有效性取决于它融入更广泛的运营生态系统的程度。”

乌克兰在将人工智能融入军事行动方面发挥着重要作用。 例如，三月份，该国国防部启动了一项首个将人工智能纳入国防流程的计划。

乌克兰国家支持的创新平台Brave1的首席执行官Andrii Hrytseniuk表示，在战场上，乌克兰在利用人工智能支持决策、无人机导航、终端制导和精确度等功能方面取得了实质性进展。

Hrytseniuk 今年春天在基辅告诉 Business Insider，当时有 200 多家当地公司正在为无人机、导弹、雷达和其他系统开发基于人工智能的组件。

乌克兰国防公司正在不同程度地将人工智能集成到他们的产品中。 许多人坚持认为机器不会从头到尾控制无人机。

流行的 Sting 拦截无人机的制造商 Wild Hornets 在 5 月份告诉《商业内幕》，人工智能将逐渐融入飞行操作的几乎每个阶段：目标检测、识别，以及后来的终端制导。

该公司发言人表示，人类仍然会根据自己的打击内容做出决定。 他们说，由于俄罗斯不断改变其战术，拦截弹操作员必须密切关注这些变化并做出必要的调整。

随着自主系统在乌克兰战场上变得越来越普遍，指挥官们同样告诉《商业内幕》，人类需要保持在循环中。

例如，地面机器人越来越多地取代士兵并承担起极其致命的前线后勤角色。 乌克兰指挥官表示，发展机器的目的是为了拯救生命，但并不是将人类完全从战场上消除。

格雷克是第 21 无人系统“海妖”团的机器人连指挥官，他要求仅通过呼号来识别身份，他表示，目标是“让人们专注于人类判断最有价值的任务”。

美国陆军军官强调，北约正在利用乌克兰的作战环境为未来潜在对抗的军事规划提供信息。

“我们不会效仿乌克兰，”上尉说。 罗南·塞夫顿。 “我们正在向乌克兰学习。”
